_about: Deeper features (500+ words) for 9 stories. New facts researched 2026-10-16 from the listed sources (two per fact unless marked as one source and hedged in the text). Where two reliable sources disagree, the text says so.

bass-reeves.excerpt: He could not read a warrant, so he memorised it. Bass Reeves wore a deputy marshal's badge for 32 years, and once served one on his own son.
sections: Born enslaved, free in the Territory

Bass Reeves was born into slavery in Crawford County, Arkansas, in July 1838. The family that enslaved him, the Reeves family of William S. Reeves, moved to Grayson County, Texas, in 1846. When the Civil War came, Reeves became a fugitive. He found refuge in Indian Territory, the land that is now Oklahoma, among the Creek and Seminole nations, and learned their customs. Exactly how and why he left Texas is not known; the sources call the stories about it legends.

Two of the sources say it "is believed" that he served with Union Indian regiments during the war. That is as far as the evidence goes, so it is not stated here as fact. After the war he settled in Van Buren, Arkansas, as a farmer, with his wife Jennie and a growing family. He also guided deputy U.S. marshals who had business in the Territory, and by his own account came to know it "like a cook knows her kitchen".
Judge Parker's court

In 1875 Judge Isaac C. Parker took over the federal court at Fort Smith, Arkansas, with a mandate to bring order to Indian Territory. He hired about 200 deputies that year. One was Bass Reeves, one of the first Black federal lawmen west of the Mississippi River. Of all those deputies, Reeves was the only one on record who started with Parker's court in 1875 and was still working when Oklahoma became a state in 1907.

He was about six feet two inches tall and weighed 180 pounds, an expert with both pistol and rifle, and he could not read or write. So before he rode out he had his warrants and writs read to him, and memorised them. The court's jurisdiction covered more than 75,000 square miles; a deputy's round trip to the western forts could run 800 miles, with a wagon, a cook and at least one posseman.
Thirty-two years, three thousand arrests

Reeves served 32 years as a deputy U.S. marshal. In November 1901 a Territory newspaper, the Chickasaw Enterprise, reported that he had arrested more than 3,000 men and women. He said the most he ever took in at once was nineteen horse thieves near Fort Sill. The outlaw Belle Starr turned herself in at Fort Smith after learning that Reeves held the warrant for her.

He was in numerous gunfights and was never wounded. He said he had killed fourteen men in self-defence; when he died, newspapers put the number at twenty. In 1887 Reeves himself stood trial for murder, for shooting his trail cook, and was found not guilty. The popular claim that he never arrested the wrong man comes from a source that only says it "is said", and the theory that he inspired the Lone Ranger has never been proven, so neither is repeated here as fact.
The hardest warrant

In 1902 came the warrant no lawman would want. His son Bennie was charged with murdering his wife. Reeves took the warrant himself and brought his son in. Bennie was convicted and sent to the federal prison at Leavenworth, Kansas. Later retellings describe a long manhunt; a newspaper report of the time says Bennie surrendered. The Oklahoma Historical Society calls the arrest the greatest testimony to his devotion to duty.
Muskogee

His first wife, Jennie, died in Fort Smith in 1896, and in 1900 he married Winnie Sumter. When Oklahoma became a state in 1907, his federal job ended; he was 67. He joined the Muskogee city police for about two years. Residents later said that not one crime was reported on his beat.

Bass Reeves died in Muskogee on 12 January 1910, of Bright's disease. In 2012 a bronze statue of him was dedicated in Fort Smith, and in December 2024 his portrait was unveiled at the Arkansas State Capitol, the first official portrait of an African American displayed there.

bessie-coleman.excerpt: American flight schools wouldn't teach her. So she learned French, sailed to France, and came home the first African American woman with a pilot's licence.
sections: Waxahachie

Bessie Coleman was born in Texas in 1892, the National Women's History Museum gives the date as 26 January, in a one-room cabin in Waxahachie, one of thirteen children of sharecropper parents who could neither read nor write. She started school in 1898, walking four miles each way to a one-room segregated schoolhouse, and was its best maths student. Every year the cotton harvest closed the school and she worked in the fields. When her father left the family in 1901, her mother took work as a cook and housekeeper.
She managed one semester at Langston Industrial College in Oklahoma before the money ran out. So she went north to Chicago, where two of her brothers lived.
A manicurist decides to fly

In Chicago she trained at a beauty school and became a popular manicurist. She survived the Chicago race riot of 1919. That year, at 27, she listened to her brother John, back from the war in France, describe women flying there, and decided she would fly too.

Almost every flying school in the United States turned her down, because she was Black and because she was a woman. Robert S. Abbott, publisher of the Chicago Defender, gave her the advice that changed her life: learn French, and apply to a French school. She did. She opened a beauty parlour to raise money, received a passport on 9 November 1920, and sailed from New York eleven days later.
Le Crotoy

In France she enrolled at the Caudron brothers' flying school at Le Crotoy, on the Somme coast, for a ten-month course in fragile early biplanes. After seven months she took the test for an international licence. On 15 June 1921 the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale issued it. The document survives in the Smithsonian's collection. Bessie Coleman was the first African American woman to hold a pilot's licence.
Queen Bess

She returned to New York in September 1921 and made her living as a stunt flier, flying loops and figure eights at air shows, and lecturing to encourage Black Americans into aviation. She returned to Chicago in 1922 as "Queen Bess, Daredevil Aviatrix"; her Chicago debut drew more than 2,000 people. She walked off a New York film set when she decided the film's portrayal of Black people was demeaning, and lost her sponsor with it.

She also refused to perform for segregated crowds. In Waxahachie, her home town, she would not fly until the show agreed to a single entrance for Black and white spectators. In Orlando she threatened to pull out of a parachute jump when she learned the event was for white people only, and the organisers opened it to Black spectators.

Flying was dangerous. After she bought a war-surplus Curtiss "Jenny", it crashed after take-off from Santa Monica, in 1923 according to the Smithsonian, and she was left with a broken leg, cracked ribs and cuts. She recovered, and she flew again.
Jacksonville, 30 April 1926

Coleman was saving to open a flight school for Black pilots. In April 1926 she went to Jacksonville, Florida, for a show. On 30 April, during a test flight with her mechanic William Wills at the controls, she sat in the rear cockpit, unbelted so that she could lean out and scout a site for a parachute jump. At about 3,000 feet the plane flipped. She fell, and died; Wills died in the crash. The National Women's History Museum says a loose wrench had jammed the controls. She was 34.

Thousands came to her funeral in Chicago; Ida B. Wells-Barnett presided. Two quotes often attributed to Coleman rest on a single source each and are not repeated here. From 1931, Black pilots flew over her grave each year and dropped flowers. A postage stamp honoured her in 1995, and in 2023 the US Mint issued a Bessie Coleman quarter. When Mae Jemison became the first African American woman in space, in 1992, she carried a picture of Bessie Coleman with her.

booker-t-washington.excerpt: One dinner with the President. The South exploded, and the President never invited him back.
sections: From slavery to Tuskegee

Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia in 1856. After the Civil War he fought hard for an education, at the Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute and then at Wayland Seminary. In 1881 he founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, a school to train Black teachers, and he headed it for the rest of his life, building it into one of the leading schools for Black Americans. In 1896 he recruited a young scientist, George Washington Carver, to lead Tuskegee's agricultural work.

By 1901 Washington was the most famous Black man in America. His 1895 speech in Atlanta, in which he urged Black Southerners to accept segregation for now and build through work and education, made him acceptable to white audiences; the Theodore Roosevelt Center notes that in private he was a lifelong supporter of civil rights efforts. His autobiography, Up From Slavery, was a best-seller. He had founded the National Negro Business League in 1900, and he wrote six books.
16 October 1901

Theodore Roosevelt became president in September 1901, after the assassination of William McKinley, and in those first months he held dinners nearly every night to talk politics. On 16 October 1901, only weeks into his presidency and a few days before the official mourning for McKinley ended, he invited Washington to dine at the White House. His purpose was practical: he wanted Washington's advice on federal appointments in the South.

Washington arrived at the north door at eight o'clock. The White House Historical Association records one other guest, Philip B. Stewart of Colorado, and says the party was probably served in the State Dining Room, since the men wore evening dress. The guests remembered a simple, cordial evening.
The firestorm

The next day, a routine listing of White House guests went out through the Associated Press, and the dinner became the biggest news since the assassination. White Southern newspapers erupted. The Atlanta Constitution called it "an insult to white civilization". The Memphis Scimitar called it "an outrage". Senator Benjamin Tillman of South Carolina made a public statement that the Roosevelt Presidential Library describes as openly murderous, and some Southerners called for the President's impeachment. Northern papers were divided. The Theodore Roosevelt Center describes the reaction as a firestorm, and says it stunned Roosevelt.

The dinner is often called the first time a Black guest dined at the White House. The White House Historical Association says the furore was tied to its being the first time an African American was entertained there; other sources word the claim differently, so it is given here as they give it.
Never invited back

In private letters Roosevelt defended his right to invite whomever he wished. But he never invited another Black American to dine at the White House in his remaining seven years in office, and his consultations with Black leaders stayed private from then on. Washington remained his adviser; his counsel lay behind Roosevelt's defence of William Crum's appointment in Charleston, and Roosevelt closed the post office at Indianola, Mississippi, rather than give in to the ousting of its Black postmistress, Minnie Cox. In January 1906 Roosevelt visited Tuskegee. Washington went on advising President Taft as well.
What one meal showed

Booker T. Washington died in 1915, with a new generation, organised in the NAACP, demanding rights openly rather than waiting for them. The school he founded still stands. One meal, and the reaction to it, showed how far the country had to go.
